title: What Studying at Johns Hopkins Taught Me
paragraphs: For nine weeks, from March 27 to May 26, I did clerkships in endocrinology and metabolism and in medical oncology at Johns Hopkins Hospital. Both were highly academic, with an intensive clerkship content.

The first half was the clerkship in endocrinology and metabolism, with outpatient clinics in the morning and the ward in the afternoon. In the outpatient clinic, I accompanied the fellows and interns at first visits and received guidance from the attending. Once I got used to it, I was allowed to do first-visit examinations by myself. I felt fulfilled in an environment where I could learn in the clinical setting about diseases such as MEN and MODY, and even NIFT-P, whose classification was proposed only in recent years. Dr. Cooper, an authority on thyroid cancer who was a central doctor in drafting the guidelines, taught me a great many things, from knowledge about the diseases to tips for examination. It was also a valuable opportunity to face patients of various races, nationalities and life backgrounds and to see directly how the doctors responded to their diverse needs. Sometimes patients broke down in tears during the interview because of the severity of their symptoms, and I felt frustrated and powerless that all I could say was "I am really sorry...".

On the ward, the work was responding to consults from other departments. I was in charge of one or two patients a day, and did rounds, presented to the attending and wrote chart notes. At first I was feeling my way while consulting guidelines on things such as how to control blood glucose and hormones after endocrine tumor surgery, but with the doctors' guidance my understanding deepened and I became accustomed to thinking logically. Sometimes I was asked to present on patients I was not in charge of, which was tense...

From partway through the fifth week, the clerkship in medical oncology began. In oncology, I was assigned to the solid tumor team, and unlike in endocrinology, the clerkship was mainly on the ward. I was always in charge of two to three inpatients with various cancers, and from admission to discharge did morning and evening rounds, charting and presentations at the general rounds. Patients' conditions varied, from relatively stable patients admitted for chemotherapy to those admitted urgently in a terminal state. Just as I felt relieved after finishing my presentations at the morning general rounds with the doctors, I would investigate the history of a newly admitted patient, take the history and examine them, check the treatment against the guidelines and UpToDate, and make a short- to long-term treatment plan, and the time passed like an arrow. While learning about diseases and treatment, I felt that being allowed to take part in discussions about the clinical trials that the doctors themselves lead was very educational. Another thing that left a deep impression on me was how to approach patients with complex backgrounds. I was taught what to think about and how to act in difficult situations, such as examining a patient admitted urgently in great distress with the least possible burden, and explaining the condition to a patient in a severe situation, and it was an extremely valuable experience. As my clerkship in oncology deepened, helped also by my experience in endocrinology, patients came to open their hearts to me more often, and near the end of the clerkship a patient sometimes told me what they really thought, saying "To be honest only with you...". In the second half, once I could do the ward clerkship faster than at first, I asked to sit in on the doctors' outpatient clinics. Each outpatient slot took about one hour per patient, and it was impressive that the doctors explained the condition and the plan very carefully and that the patients themselves asked many questions.

In parallel with the clerkships in endocrinology and metabolism and in oncology, I was also looked after by the pancreatic cancer laboratory of Dr. Michael Goggins. Dr. 田村 and Dr. 阿部, who were doing postdoctoral research abroad from the First Department of Surgery at Kyushu University, mainly guided me, and I was able to take part in the experimental work too. While overwhelmed by the doctors from many different countries and by the laboratory with three next-generation sequencers and nearly ten PCR thermal cyclers, the time in which the fun of research work I had not done for a while, such as PCR and electrophoresis, was reawakened was fulfilling, separately from the clinical work.

What I learned during these nine weeks was far more than I had imagined and became irreplaceable. The clerkship period, in which I learned clinical work and research in parallel and witnessed a wide variety of treatments from major diseases to rare ones, was fulfilling every day. I am convinced that I had a wonderful experience.

I am truly full of gratitude to Dr. 粕谷 and Dr. 長谷川 and the professors of Nagoya University who gave me great support over a long period, from the preparation period before the study abroad through the stay and after returning, the professors of Johns Hopkins, Dr. 田村 and Dr. 阿部 of Kyushu University, 西尾さん, the administrative staff, and the many others who gave great support. I will treasure this valuable experience for life and make use of it in my future. Thank you very much.
